prompt: You have 90 minutes before a flight and just got to the airport. What do you do first?

options.A: Check in at the counter even though you have a mobile boarding pass.
options.B: Head straight to security; you already have your boarding pass on your phone.
options.C: Grab coffee first; security lines are unpredictable anyway.
options.D: Sit at the gate area first to see if there are delays.

prompt: A teammate proposes a new abstraction layer that would save ~50 LOC across three call sites but adds a new file and a small mental cost. You:

options.A: Accept it; less code is less code.
options.B: Reject it; YAGNI — the savings don't justify the indirection at three sites.
options.C: Ask for a fourth use case before merging.
options.D: Merge it but inline the helper at the call sites instead.

prompt: Two equally-qualified candidates: one with 10 years at one company, one with 10 years across five companies. Which do you lean toward for a senior IC role?

options.A: The single-company candidate; deep context matters most.
options.B: The five-company candidate; breadth of patterns matters most.
options.C: Neither matters; only the interview signal does.
options.D: The five-company candidate, but probe for tenure-vs-flight signals.

prompt: Your PR is blocked by a CI flake on a test you didn't touch. The retry button is right there. You:

options.A: Retry once; if it passes, merge.
options.B: Retry once; if it passes, merge — but file a flaky-test issue.
options.D: Skip the test with a TODO and merge.

prompt: Reading a paper. The methods section is dense. You:

options.A: Read it linearly start to finish.
options.B: Skim the abstract, then jump to results, then back to methods.
options.C: Start with the figures; methods only if the figures interest you.
options.D: Read the introduction and conclusion first, methods last.

prompt: A friend asks if they should ship a feature that's 'mostly done' or polish it for another week. The feature isn't critical. You say:

options.A: Ship it; perfect is the enemy of done.
options.B: Polish it; the second week is where quality lives.
options.C: Depends on the cost of being wrong — is it reversible?
options.D: Show it to two users first, then decide.

prompt: You're given a budget of 5 hours and have a 12-hour task. What's your first move?

options.A: Start working and see how far you get.
options.B: Cut scope by 60% before writing any code.
options.C: Ask for more time before committing.
options.D: Identify the 20% of the task that delivers 80% of the value.

prompt: A model proposes a refactor that touches 30 files. Tests pass. You:

options.A: Accept it — green tests are green tests.
options.B: Reject it — too much surface for one change.
options.C: Ask it to split into per-file commits.
options.D: Read every diff manually before merging.

prompt: Someone asks for your advice on a decision you have a strong opinion on. They've already made the opposite decision. You:

options.A: Tell them your opinion anyway — they asked.
options.B: Validate their choice; the decision is made.
options.C: Tell them your opinion but frame it as 'what I'd do' not 'what you should do'.
options.D: Ask what made them choose that way before sharing.

prompt: Your test suite takes 8 minutes. You can either spend a day cutting it to 2 minutes, or accept the 8 minutes. The suite runs ~5x/day.

options.B: Accept it; 8 minutes isn't worth a day of work.
options.C: Cut the slowest 2 tests only; quick win.
options.D: Cut it AND fix the underlying coupling causing slow tests.
